title: The way to Brahma
hookLine: Subha asks about householder and renunciant; the four immeasurables as the way to Brahma

lines: THE HOUSEHOLDER OR THE ONE WHO LEAVES?
cards: A young brahmin named Subha is staying in Sāvatthī on business. He comes to the Buddha with a question that still turns up at kitchen tables.
Who does better, the person who stays in the world, with a job and a family, or the person who leaves it all for a spiritual life?
The brahmins of his day, he says, hold that the householder is the one who accomplishes what is good. What does the Buddha say? He answers by refusing to give a one-word answer.

teach.b: On this, the Buddha says, I'm one who analyzes; I don't speak one-sidedly. A householder who lives badly doesn't accomplish the good, and neither does a monk who lives badly.

A householder or a monk who lives well, either can. Then the talk turns to Brahmā, the high god the brahmins hoped to be united with after death. Subha has heard that the Buddha knows the way to companionship with Brahmā.
The Buddha says: suppose a man was born and raised in a village called Naḷakāra, not far from here. If someone asked him the way to Naḷakāra, would he hesitate? No, he grew up there.
In the same way, the Buddha says, I know Brahmā and the way there. So Subha asks: teach me the way. And the Buddha describes four states of heart.
A person fills one direction with a mind of loving-kindness, then the second, the third, the fourth, then above, below, across, everywhere, a mind abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility.
Then compassion, the same way. Then appreciative joy, gladness at others' good. Then equanimity.
These are the four immeasurables, also called the brahmavihāras, the dwellings of Brahmā. When the heart is freed like this, the Buddha says, no limited action remains there.
And he gives a picture: a strong conch-blower makes himself heard in all four directions without effort.
That's the way to Brahmā in this sutta: not a ritual, not a birth, but a heart grown so wide it has no edges. Subha leaves delighted, and goes for refuge.

how: The four brahmavihāras, loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy and equanimity, are practiced across Buddhist traditions, often by radiating each one toward oneself, loved ones, strangers, difficult people and all beings in every direction.

o: a heaven where Brahmā's followers live after death
the four immeasurables, dwellings of Brahmā
a temple where brahmins worship the god Brahmā

games.q: the way to Brahmā: tap the pairs.
p: knows the way home without hesitating

s: the Buddha says only monks can accomplish the good
he says either can, if they live well, and neither can if they live badly.
the four immeasurables are also called the dwellings of Brahmā
brahmavihāra: the abodes or dwellings of Brahmā.
in this sutta the way to Brahmā is a ritual performed by priests
it's a heart of kindness, compassion, joy and equanimity spread without limit.

games.q: Subha asks: who does better, the one who stays home or the one who leaves for the spiritual life? what does the Buddha answer?
o: it depends on how each one lives
games.why: 'I'm one who analyzes,' he says. either can live well or badly. the answer isn't in the role but in the life.

practice: Choose one immeasurable, kindness, compassion, gladness at others' good, or steady equanimity, and feel it first toward someone easy.
Then let it spread the way the sutta says, in front of you, behind, to the sides, above and below, until it has no edge. If your mind wanders, start again with the easy person.

wordCard.voice: Brahmavihara. Loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy and equanimity, spread in every direction without limit: the dwellings of Brahmā.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit brahmavihāra: dwelling of Brahmā, the name for the four immeasurables.

carryVoice: Your line: a heart with no edges. Like a conch heard in all four directions. Until tomorrow.
